positive_control_fresh_copies.evidence: fresh schemas are identical copies of baseline; Jaccard=1.0 by construction

null_control_noise_no_usage_drop.observed: noise usage_similarity = 1.0 for all 3 noise patterns at all 4 sizes

stable_resource_control.expected: Not applicable (no users_stable resource in this experiment)
stable_resource_control.evidence: Experiment uses field-usage profiling, not per-resource drift detection

observations: Field-usage profiling successfully discriminates remove_field and required_to_optional from noise: both produce usage_similarity < 0.90 while all noise patterns produce usage_similarity = 1.0.

change_type does NOT reduce usage_similarity (remains 1.0 at all sizes) because the server still returns the field — clients receive the field regardless of type change. This is a genuine limitation: field-usage profiling measures field AVAILABILITY, not TYPE COMPATIBILITY.

The discrimination gap (noise_usage_mean - drift_usage_mean = 0.165) is substantial and exceeds the 0.05 threshold, indicating meaningful separation between noise and drift in the usage-similarity dimension.

Pearson r = -0.045 between Jaccard and usage-similarity confirms the signals are nearly uncorrelated (orthogonal). Usage-similarity provides information that Jaccard cannot: noise drops Jaccard to ~0.91 while usage_sim stays at 1.0; required_to_optional drops Jaccard to ~0.82-0.96 but usage_sim drops much further to ~0.64.

Per-profile analysis reveals asymmetric impact: Profile A (identity-only) is most affected by required_to_optional (usage_sim=0.5) because it depends on only 2 fields, losing 1 reduces Jaccard to 0.5. Profile C (full-profile) is least affected (usage_sim=0.75) because it has more fields to fall back on.

The experiment is FALSIFIED because change_type fails Condition 1: type-only changes do not alter field availability and thus cannot be detected by usage-similarity alone. This is a measurement-valid negative, not an infrastructure failure.
validity_notes: Mock server returns deterministic responses with no timing jitter, network variation, or stochastic field availability. Real-world usage-similarity may be noisier.
Client profiles are hand-designed (3 profiles: light/medium/heavy). Real clients may use overlapping or unusual field subsets.
Noise patterns deliberately target fields NOT in any client profile. If real-world noise affected used fields, usage-similarity would drop under noise — potentially closing the discrimination gap.

The change_type pattern changes a non-id field's type but the field is still present and non-null. A more realistic model might have clients validate types and reject incompatible ones, which would reduce usage-similarity for type drift. This was not modeled in the current experiment.

required_to_optional is modeled by removing the field from ~50% of responses (resource_id % 2 == 0). The 50% missing rate is arbitrary; different rates would produce different usage-similarity values.

Sample size N=30 per condition is sufficient for the observed zero-variance conditions (noise, change_type) but may be insufficient for the non-zero-variance conditions (remove_field std~0.055, required_to_optional std~0.0).

Structural Jaccard is computed on (field_path, type) pairs as in prior experiments. Usage-similarity is computed as mean per-profile Jaccard(field_used_fresh, field_used_stale). These are different Jaccard computations on different object types.
unresolved: Whether client-side type validation (rejecting fields with unexpected types) would make change_type detectable by usage-similarity. This would require modeling type schemas and client validation logic.
Whether usage-similarity discrimination holds when noise patterns affect fields that clients actually use (not just unused fields). The current noise model is adversarially favorable.
Whether real APIs with DB/cache/CDN effects produce usage-similarity values that match or differ from the deterministic mock.
Whether composite signals (Jaccard + usage-similarity + type-compatibility) could detect all three drift patterns simultaneously.
The optimal number and diversity of client profiles for generalizing usage-similarity discrimination to real-world heterogeneous API consumers.
Whether the required_to_optional detection (usage_sim ~0.64) generalizes to real-world optional fields where the field is present for authenticated users but absent for unauthenticated ones.
